member.name: M:Gordic.Wfl.WinClientTest.VirusUtils.Check(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Invokes the installed virus scanner(s) using the Internal.ShObjIdl.IAttachmentExecute service, which, when set up correctly, delete infected files. If the implementation throws an exception, we wrap it in a . There is no defined behavior though.
member.param: the full path and name of the file
if not null, it will be used in the exception text, otherwise, we'll use the filename

remarks.para: Inspected behavior of some antivirus products after disabling them, downloading the EICAR test file, reenabling them and calling this function:

item.description: When it's set to scan downloads and attachments, it returns 0x80004005, and when automatic actions are enabled, it deletes the file immediately, before returning.
Same as Windows Defender, no surprise there.

It's only invoked when document protection is set up to be integrated into the system. It always returns zero, so no exception is thrown, but it deletes the infected file immediately, before returning.

remarks.para: This function only tries to guarantee that if an antivirus software is installed and set up correctly, then infected files will be deleted, but the caller can't be sure what happened, because some products never throw an exception. Checking for the deletion of the file is unreliable because it might be deleted for other reasons, given an arbitrary filename we can't be sure that noone else is using it. Callers would also need to account for the fact that under normal circumstances, if you don't temporarily disable your antivirus software, you can't even create an infected file in any way because of the realtime protection, but creating a file can also fail for other reasons, too. So if you really want to know if a file contains a virus or not, this is not way to go, see the other overload.

member.param: describes what the contents are, we use it in the exception message

remarks.para: This function's main goal is to trigger the realtime file access scanning of antivirus products and differentiate the results from other types if I/O or security errors, but to be on the safe side, we also invoke the other overload. So if either realtime or on-demand attachment scanning is turned on, calling this overload will determine quite precisely if the contents are infected or not.

We create a new temporary file. As opposed to the other overload, which takes an arbitrary filename, here we know that the temporary file we use is just ours and shouldn't just be deleted by someone else. We also set up an ACL to ensure that noone else is able to touch the file, while also ensuring that we have full control over it. If an I/O error occurs during a file operation, it won't produce a false positive, but a security error will be reported as a virus. The chances of this method failing are very slim, even deliberately making it fail is very hard. But still, the only perfect solution is to use the specific, documented, supported API of an antivirus software.
Inspected behavior of some antivirus products after calling this function with the EICAR test file contents:

item.description: The realtime protection alone doesn't detect anything, only the attachment scanning when calling the other overload.
When only the realtime file access protection is turned on, the opening for read fails. When attachment scanning is also turned on, the other overload reports a virus.

With realtime protection, the file is deleted immediately after closing it, no need to call the other overload. With only document protection enabled, the deletion will happen after calling the other overload. We can safely detect both deletions.
